title: 塑造 2026 年游戏行业的六大监管风险指南
content:
A guide to six regulatory risks shaping games in 2026 | GamesIndustry.biz

Dr Simon Hembt is counsel at Bird & Bird in Frankfurt, Germany. He advises games companies on IP, AI/tech, and media regulation. He co-edited Bird & Bird's
Game Plan 2026
report.
Imagine a free-to-play shooter with pay-to-win in-game monetization (aka "golden bullets"), various in-game items (such as skins), voice chat, a user-generated-content (UGC) hub, and an AI companion. All relatively common features, but they represent a regulatory puzzle, since each one might be subject to a different law at national and European Union level.
The EU AI Act's rules on
"deepfakes" and the representation of real-world locations and people in games
have applied since August 2, and the first reporting obligations under the
Cyber Resilience Act
followed on September 11 – but there is more still to come, with the  European Commission announcing a further two landmark projects.
The EU KIDS Act has proposed rules on online safety that
could affect daily log-in bonuses among many other things
, while the first draft of the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) is likely to contain several different rules that affect in-game worlds. In addition, the EU Consumer Protection Cooperation Network (CPC) has started a
series of enforcement actions based on its key principles
.
Bird & Bird's international video games team has mapped the legal trends shaping games, and this article highlights six risks that studios need to be aware of, and what they can do to stay ahead.
The CPC has in-game shops in its sights
In March 2025, the CPC
acted against Swedish studio Star Stable Entertainment
, whose game Star Stable is popular with children. The CPC alleged that the game uses, among other things, incentives for kids to buy items, unclear currency pricing, and undisclosed influencer marketing.
The CPC acted against Star Stable in 2025  |
Image credit:
Star Stable Entertainment
The same month, the CPC published its
Key Principles on In-Game Virtual Currencies
. The basic idea is that consumer law covers every purchase made with a virtual currency bought with real money.
These seven key principles cover:
Clear and transparent pricing by showing the real-world money price (for example, in euros).
No cost-obscuring practices (for example, multiple currency layers).
No forced surplus purchases (for example, players should not be urged to spend extra money through odd pricing of bundles).
Clear pre-contractual information.
The right of withdrawal to cancel purchases and get refunds for unused virtual currencies.
Fair and understandable terms in plain language.
The protection of vulnerable groups.
Since the end of September, the EU and national authorities have conducted
coordinated actions
to enforce these principles.
The EU AI Act now enforces transparency
After the backlash over AI outputs identified by players, the issue has become rather sensitive, but studios now have a legal obligation around making AI use clear in some cases.
Providing a generative AI system, such as a text-to-image model, triggers an obligation by the provider to mark its output in a machine-readable way and make it detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act). A studio offering players its own AI tool for creating UGC would usually be considered as the provider. This obligation began in August, although the grace period for systems already on the market runs until December 2, 2026.
The EU AI Act covers real-world representations  |
Image credit:
Ubisoft
Deepfakes created with third-party AI tools (which can cover representations of real-world locations, people, or events) might also need labelling in some cases. However, certain exceptions could see the obligation waived, or, in an evidently creative work, a notice in the credits might suffice.
Article 50(1) of the AI Act requires providers of interactive AI systems to make sure players know they are dealing with AI, unless that is obvious. These systems could include conversational bots supercharged with AI, and the "obvious" exception may cause particular headaches in games played by children, since in the Commission's view the use of AI might not be as obvious to children as it is to adults.
Before launch, video game providers should list every AI feature in each title and work out its potential regulation.
The Digital Services Act has tightened the rules for UGC
A video games provider that stores UGC such as pictures, texts, or designs on its servers will be deemed a hosting service under the Digital Services Act (DSA), and making this UGC publicly available to all players is likely to make the provider an online platform.
The DSA provides for a tiered regime with new obligations for each tier (for example, intermediary, hosting service, online platform, and very large online platform). In August, the Commission
designated Roblox as a very large online platform
, the category with the strictest duties.
The DSA does not make video game providers check every upload. Providers are generally not liable for illegal uploads they are not aware of, as long as they act quickly once they are. Players also need an easy way to report in-game content, and anyone whose UGC the provider removes or restricts must get a statement of reasons. AI creation tools raise the stakes, because players can now produce infringing or harmful content at scale. A report button alone might no longer be enough.
For many online platform games, however, Article 28 of the DSA is key. Online platforms that minors can access have to take appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security for them: An "18+ clause" buried in the terms and conditions will not take the provider out of scope. guidelines from July 2025
